questions.question: A system has three independent components in series, each with 99% availability. What is the approximate overall system availability?

options.text: 99% (the weakest component determines availability)
97% (availabilities multiply for serial dependencies)
99.9% (redundancy improves overall availability)
95% (each component adds 1-2% unavailability)

questions.explanation: For components in series (all must work), multiply availabilities: 0.99 × 0.99 × 0.99 ≈ 0.97 (97%). Each additional serial component reduces overall availability. This is why microservices architectures with many synchronous dependencies can have surprisingly low end-to-end availability. Amazon's internal guidance suggests keeping synchronous call chains short—a 10-service chain with 99.9% per-service availability yields only 99% end-to-end availability. The mathematical principle: P(A AND B AND C) = P(A) × P(B) × P(C) for independent events.

questions.question: A critical service requires 99.99% availability. The team proposes adding a redundant instance. If each instance has 99% availability and they operate in active-passive mode with instant failover, what is the combined availability?

options.text: 99% (limited by the active instance)
99.99% (parallel redundancy dramatically improves availability)
99.5% (failover adds some improvement but not multiplicative)
98.01% (redundancy helps but both could fail together)

questions.explanation: For parallel redundancy (either can serve): 1 - (1-0.99)² = 1 - 0.0001 = 0.9999 (99.99%). Both must fail simultaneously for system failure. This is the mathematical foundation of high availability—two 'two nines' components achieve 'four nines' together. AWS Availability Zones use this principle: each AZ might have 99.9% availability, but multi-AZ deployments achieve 99.99%+. The formula generalizes: with N redundant components each at availability A, combined availability = 1 - (1-A)^N.

questions.question: Which practices contribute to achieving high availability? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Deploying across multiple availability zones
Implementing health checks and automatic failover
Maximizing resource utilization to reduce infrastructure costs
Designing for graceful degradation under partial failures

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ deployment, health checks with failover, and graceful degradation all improve availability. However, maximizing resource utilization actually hurts availability—systems running at 90%+ utilization have no headroom for traffic spikes or recovery operations. Google's SRE book recommends keeping services at 50-70% utilization for this reason. Netflix's approach includes 'reserved capacity' specifically to handle failures without cascading. The tradeoff between cost efficiency and availability is fundamental to capacity planning.

questions.question: An e-commerce site targets 99.9% availability (three nines). During a planned maintenance window, the site will be down for 2 hours. How much additional unplanned downtime can they afford for the rest of the year?

options.text: Approximately 6.7 hours (8.76 total minus 2 planned)
Approximately 8.76 hours (planned maintenance typically excluded from SLA)
Zero hours (any downtime violates the SLA)
Approximately 4.76 hours (planned counts double against SLA)

questions.explanation: 99.9% allows ~8.76 hours/year downtime (0.1% of 8,760 hours). With 2 hours planned maintenance counted, ~6.76 hours remain for unplanned outages. However, many SLAs explicitly exclude scheduled maintenance from calculations—check your specific SLA terms. Google Cloud's SLA excludes 'scheduled downtime' while AWS counts all downtime. This distinction matters enormously for operations planning. The calculation: 8,760 hours/year × 0.001 = 8.76 hours maximum downtime for three nines.

questions.question: A payment processing system experiences a database failover that takes 30 seconds. During this time, all transactions fail. Which availability pattern would minimize this impact?

options.text: Cold standby with automated provisioning
Warm standby with asynchronous replication
Hot standby with synchronous replication
Multi-master replication with conflict resolution

questions.explanation: Hot standby with synchronous replication keeps the standby fully synchronized and ready, minimizing failover time to seconds or sub-seconds. Cold standby requires provisioning time (minutes). Warm standby with async replication risks data loss and still needs promotion time. Multi-master could work but adds complexity around conflict resolution for financial transactions. Stripe and Square use synchronous replication for payment data—the latency cost of sync replication is acceptable given the criticality of zero data loss and fast failover for financial transactions.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between availability and reliability?

options.text: They are mathematically equivalent metrics measured on different scales
High reliability is necessary and sufficient for high availability
A system can be highly available while having low reliability
Reliability measures uptime while availability measures correctness

questions.explanation: A system can be highly available (always accessible) but not reliable (frequently returns errors or wrong results). Reliability is about correct operation; availability is about being operational. Consider a web service that's always up (100% available) but returns incorrect data 10% of the time (90% reliable). Conversely, a highly reliable system that's frequently down for maintenance has low availability. Amazon's retail site prioritizes availability—showing cached/stale data during outages rather than error pages. The definitions: Availability = uptime/(uptime+downtime); Reliability = correct_operations/total_operations.

questions.question: A microservices architecture has 20 services, each with 99.5% availability. If a user request requires all 20 services to respond synchronously, what is the approximate request success rate?

options.text: 99.5% (determined by the least available service)
90% (serial dependency multiplication)
95% (averaging effect across services)
80% (each service adds ~1% failure probability)

questions.explanation: 0.995^20 ≈ 0.905 (90.5%). This demonstrates why microservices must implement resilience patterns—serial dependencies multiply failure probabilities. A request touching 20 services, each at 'two and a half nines,' achieves less than 'one nine' end-to-end. This is why Netflix invented Hystrix (circuit breakers) and why modern architectures use async communication, caching, and graceful degradation. The mathematical reality: even excellent per-service availability compounds into poor user experience without resilience patterns.

questions.question: Which strategies help maintain availability during deployments? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Blue-green deployments with instant traffic switching
Rolling updates with health-check-gated progression
Deploying during low-traffic windows to minimize impact
Canary releases with gradual traffic shifting

questions.explanation: Blue-green, rolling updates, and canary releases all enable zero-downtime deployments through different mechanisms. Blue-green maintains two complete environments; rolling updates replace instances incrementally; canary releases test with small traffic percentages first. Deploying during low-traffic windows reduces blast radius but doesn't eliminate downtime—it's risk mitigation, not zero-downtime deployment. Facebook deploys code twice daily using canary releases; Amazon deploys every 11.7 seconds using rolling updates. The key principle: always maintain enough healthy capacity to serve traffic during deployment.

questions.question: A system architect must choose between synchronous and asynchronous replication for a database. Which trade-off is most accurate?

options.text: Synchronous provides higher availability but risks data inconsistency
Asynchronous provides higher availability but risks data loss on failover
Synchronous provides lower latency due to parallel writes
Asynchronous guarantees consistency through eventual convergence

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication doesn't wait for replica acknowledgment, providing better availability (primary isn't blocked by slow/failed replicas) and lower latency, but risks losing recent writes during failover (replication lag). Synchronous ensures consistency but can reduce availability if replicas are slow/unavailable—the primary blocks waiting for acknowledgment. PostgreSQL streaming replication offers both modes. Financial systems typically choose synchronous (data integrity over availability); social media often chooses asynchronous (availability over perfect consistency). The CAP theorem manifests here: you're choosing between C and A.

questions.question: A team claims that adding more redundant components always improves system availability. Under what circumstances is this claim FALSE?

options.text: When redundant components share a common failure mode
When failover mechanisms themselves can fail
When added complexity increases the probability of configuration errors
All of the above represent valid counterexamples

questions.explanation: Additional components add complexity, potential failure modes, and coordination overhead. Shared dependencies (same power supply, same software bug), failover mechanism failures, and configuration errors can all negate redundancy benefits. The 2017 S3 outage was caused by a configuration error during routine maintenance—more redundancy wouldn't have helped. Google's Chubby paper notes that their lock service's biggest outages came from software bugs replicated across all instances. Redundancy must be properly designed with independent failure domains, tested failover, and operational simplicity.

questions.question: A global service needs to maintain availability during regional outages. Which architecture pattern is most appropriate?

options.text: Single-region with cross-region backup replication
Multi-region active-passive with DNS failover
Multi-region active-active with global load balancing
Single-region with multiple availability zones

questions.explanation: Multi-region active-active provides the highest availability during regional outages as traffic automatically routes to healthy regions without failover delay. Active-passive requires failover time (DNS propagation can take minutes) and the passive region may have cold-start issues. Single-region solutions don't survive regional failures regardless of AZ redundancy. Netflix, Spotify, and Google all use active-active multi-region architectures. The tradeoff: active-active is operationally complex (data synchronization, conflict resolution) but provides the best availability for truly global services.

questions.question: Which factors should be included when calculating a system's availability SLA? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Planned maintenance windows (depending on SLA terms)
Partial degradation periods where some features are unavailable
Third-party dependency outages outside your control
Time to detect failures before users are impacted

questions.explanation: Comprehensive SLAs should account for all downtime sources: planned maintenance (often excluded but should be disclosed), degraded operation (partial availability is still reduced availability), external dependencies (your users don't care whose fault it is), and detection delays (MTTD is part of total downtime). AWS and GCP SLAs define 'unavailability' precisely—read the fine print. Slack's SLA counts partial degradation; Salesforce's excludes scheduled maintenance. How each factor is counted varies by SLA definition, but all affect real user experience.
